LLC DEFAULT OPERATING RULES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, LLC

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, states what California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.01 et seq.) provides about the rules that govern a limited liability company's internal affairs when its members have not addressed a given matter in a written operating agreement — or have no written operating agreement at all. Where a specific business name is named below, that is Acme, LLC; this sheet can also be read on its own, without it filled in, as a general reference to what the statute says. This sheet states the law; it does not draft, adopt, or amend any operating agreement, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

WHAT COUNTS AS AN LLC'S "OPERATING AGREEMENT"
California's LLC statute defines "operating agreement" far more broadly than the written document that phrase usually brings to mind. By statutory definition, an operating agreement is the agreement of all of a limited liability company's members concerning the matters the statute assigns to it, and that agreement can be oral, in a record (written), implied from the members' conduct, or any combination of the three — it does not need to be called an "operating agreement," and it does not need to exist as a single signed document at all. A limited liability company with only one member can have an operating agreement too: the statute specifically provides that a single-member operating agreement is not unenforceable merely because only one person is a party to it. Separately, a person does not need to sign anything to be bound: becoming a member of a limited liability company is itself, by statute, deemed assent to whatever operating agreement already governs that company.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Operating agreement” means the agreement, whether or not referred to as an operating agreement and whether oral, in a record, implied, or in any combination thereof, of all the members of a limited liability company, including a sole member, concerning the matters described in subdivision (a) of Section 17701.10."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.02(s), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.02(s) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.02.)
  "An operating agreement of a limited liability company having only one member shall not be unenforceable by reason of there being only one person who is a party to the operating agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.02(s), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.02(s) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.02.)
  "A person that becomes a member of a limited liability company is deemed to assent to the operating agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.11(b), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.11(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.11.)
  Known gap: The statute does not supply an evidentiary standard or checklist for what a court accepts as proof of an oral or implied operating agreement's terms; where members disagree about what was orally agreed or implied from their conduct, that dispute is resolved case by case on the facts presented, not by any statutory formula, and this sheet cannot predict how a particular disagreement would come out.

WHEN THE OPERATING AGREEMENT IS SILENT, THE STATUTE FILLS THE GAP
California's LLC statute assigns four broad subjects to the operating agreement: relations among the members and between the members and the company, the rights and duties of a manager, the company's activities and the conduct of those activities, and the means and conditions for amending the operating agreement itself. Where the operating agreement — written, oral, implied, or some combination — does not address one of those subjects, the statute does not leave a void: the Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act itself governs that matter instead. This is why a limited liability company can operate lawfully with no written document at all, or with a written document that is silent on a given point: the statutory default rules described elsewhere in this sheet apply automatically to fill whatever the members have not otherwise addressed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as otherwise provided in this section, the operating agreement governs all of the following: (1) Relations among the members as members and between the members and the limited liability company. (2) The rights and duties under this title of a person in the capacity of manager. (3) The activities of the limited liability company and the conduct of those activities. (4) The means and conditions for amending the operating agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(a), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  "To the extent the operating agreement does not otherwise provide for a matter described in subdivision (a), this title governs the matter."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(b), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  Known gap: Whether a particular matter is 'addressed' by an oral or implied agreement, as opposed to left to the statutory default, is often exactly what members disagree about after the fact; the statute does not define how much specificity is needed for an informal agreement to count as addressing a subject, so that line is drawn case by case.

A STATUTORY FLOOR NO OPERATING AGREEMENT CAN WAIVE
The members' freedom to override the statutory defaults by agreement is broad but not unlimited. California's LLC statute lists specific things an operating agreement — no matter how the members word it, and regardless of unanimous consent — may not do. Among them: it may not vary the company's statutory capacity to sue and be sued in its own name, and, subject to narrow, separately-listed exceptions, it may not eliminate the duty of loyalty, the duty of care, or any other fiduciary duty a member or manager owes. It likewise may not eliminate the contractual obligation of good faith and fair dealing that the statute imposes on members and managers, though the agreement may prescribe non-manifestly-unreasonable standards for measuring that obligation. These are floor-level protections that exist independent of what the members put in writing, orally agree to, or imply through their conduct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Vary a limited liability company’s capacity under Section 17701.05 to sue and be sued in its own name."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(1), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  "eliminate the duty of loyalty, the duty of care, or any other fiduciary duty."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(4), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  "eliminate the contractual obligation of good faith and fair dealing under subdivision (d) of Section 17704.09, but the operating agreement may prescribe the standards by which the performance of the obligation is to be measured, if the standards are not manifestly unreasonable as determined at the time the standards are prescribed."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(5), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  Known gap: This sheet lists only a sample of the non-waivable list; Section 17701.10 enumerates well over a dozen additional items — covering matters like dissolution standing, merger approval rights, and records access — that this sheet does not individually restate, and the exceptions and cross-references attached to several of them (including the loyalty and care items) are more detailed than summarized here.

SOME STATUTORY DEFAULTS CAN BE CHANGED ONLY IN A WRITTEN OPERATING AGREEMENT
Not every default rule can be varied by an oral or implied operating agreement, even though oral and implied operating agreements are otherwise valid under California's LLC statute. The statute singles out certain provisions — including the liability-shield provision, the indemnification provision, and much of the meeting, notice, and voting mechanics for manager-managed companies — that may be varied only by a written operating agreement. Fiduciary duties receive an even narrower path: a member's or manager's fiduciary duties may be modified only in a written operating agreement, and only with the members' informed consent — the statute specifically states that merely becoming a member and thereby being deemed to assent to the operating agreement does not, by itself, count as the informed consent that a fiduciary-duty modification requires.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "provided, however, that the provisions of Sections 17701.13, 17703.01, and 17704.08 and subdivisions (f) to (r), inclusive, and (u) to (w), inclusive, of Section 17704.07 shall only be varied by a written operating agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(d), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  "The fiduciary duties of a manager to a manager-managed limited liability company and to the members of the limited liability company and of a member to a member-managed limited liability company and to the members of such limited liability company shall only be modified in a written operating agreement with the informed consent of the members. Assenting to the operating agreement pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 17701.11 shall not constitute informed consent."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(e), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.10.)
  Known gap: The statute's list of provisions restricted to written-agreement-only variation cross-references several other code sections by number rather than describing their content in the same sentence; a member or manager relying on an oral or implied agreement to have modified one of those specific provisions cannot determine from this clause alone whether that provision is on the restricted list.

THE DEFAULT MANAGEMENT STRUCTURE AND VOTING THRESHOLDS
Absent a contrary election, California's LLC statute makes every limited liability company member-managed by default: a company is member-managed unless its articles of organization contain the specific statement required to make it manager-managed instead. In a member-managed company, the statutory default rules are: each member has equal rights in management and conduct of the company's activities, including equal voting rights; a disagreement among members over a matter in the ordinary course of the company's activities is decided by a majority of the members; an act outside the ordinary course of the company's activities may be undertaken only with the consent of all members; and the operating agreement itself may be amended only with the consent of all members. These default thresholds — majority for ordinary matters, unanimity for extraordinary matters and for amending the operating agreement — apply automatically unless the members have provided otherwise.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A limited liability company is a member-managed limited liability company unless the articles of organization contain the statement required by paragraph (5) of subdivision (b) of Section 17702.01."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(a), Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.07.)
  "each member has equal rights in the management and conduct of the limited liability company’s activities including equal voting rights."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(2), Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.07.)
  "A difference arising among members as to a matter in the ordinary course of the activities of the limited liability company shall be decided by a majority of the members."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(3), Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.07.)
  "Except as otherwise provided in Article 10 (commencing with Section 17710.01), an act outside the ordinary course of the activities of the limited liability company may be undertaken only with the consent of all members."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(4), Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.07.)
  "The operating agreement may be amended only with the consent of all members."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(5), Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.07.)
  Known gap: The statute does not define "ordinary course of the activities" versus a matter "outside the ordinary course"; that line depends on the nature of the particular company's business and is not resolved by any bright-line statutory test, so which threshold applies to a given decision can itself be disputed among the members.

IF THE LLC ELECTS MANAGER-MANAGEMENT INSTEAD
Where the articles of organization state that the company is manager-managed, a different set of default rules applies. Any matter relating to the company's activities is decided exclusively by the managers, not the members, except where the statute expressly provides otherwise. A manager is chosen by the consent of a majority of the members and remains a manager until a successor is chosen, unless the manager resigns, is removed, or dies (or, for a manager that is not an individual, terminates); the members may remove a manager at any time, without cause, by majority consent, subject to any service contract the manager has with the company. A person does not need to be a member to serve as manager, but if a member who is also a manager dissociates as a member, that dissociation removes the person as manager as well.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "any matter relating to the activities of the limited liability company is decided exclusively by the managers."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(1), Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.07.)
  "A manager may be chosen at any time by the consent of a majority of the members and remains a manager until a successor has been chosen, unless the manager at an earlier time resigns, is removed, or dies, or, in the case of a manager that is not an individual, terminates. A manager may be removed at any time by the consent of a majority of the members without cause, subject to the rights, if any, of the manager under any service contract with the limited liability company."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(5), Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.07.)
  "A person need not be a member to be a manager, but the dissociation of a member that is also a manager removes the person as a manager."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(6), Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(6) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.07.)
  Known gap: This describes only the default management-authority and manager-selection rules; the same section separately imposes detailed meeting, notice, quorum, and written-consent mechanics for manager-managed companies (several of which, per the written-agreement clause above, can only be varied in writing) that are not restated here.

WHEN A FILED RECORD CONFLICTS WITH THE OPERATING AGREEMENT
A limited liability company's articles of organization and other records filed with the Secretary of State are not the same thing as its operating agreement, and the two can conflict — for example, where a filed record states a management structure or authority that differs from what the members actually agreed among themselves. California's statute resolves that conflict differently depending on who is asking: as among the members, dissociated members, transferees, and managers, the operating agreement prevails. As to other persons — typically third parties dealing with the company — the filed record prevails, but only to the extent they reasonably rely on it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The operating agreement prevails as to members, dissociated members, transferees, and managers."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.12(d)(1), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.12(d)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.12.)
  "The record prevails as to other persons to the extent they reasonably rely on the record."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.12(d)(2), Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.12(d)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.12.)
  Known gap: The statute does not define what counts as "reasonable" reliance on a filed record by a third party; that determination is fact-specific and this sheet cannot say in advance how a particular third party's reliance would be assessed.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
I, Jordan Lee, certify that I prepared this information sheet as a summary of Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.01 et seq. and the statutes it cross-references, for informational reference only. This information sheet does not draft, adopt, or amend any operating agreement for Acme, LLC, does not determine what Acme, LLC's members have or have not agreed to among themselves, and is not a substitute for consulting a person licensed to practice law in the relevant jurisdiction.

Business name under consideration, if applicable: Acme, LLC

Executed on September 6, 2026 at San Jose, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________
